media:group.media:description:
We don’t wait for the future. We engineer it.
From the mountains to the sea, NC State’s College of Engineering is building what’s next for North Carolina and beyond. Advanced sensors and AI that protect farmers’ crops from disease. Intelligent robotics that help people walk again. Drones that can find a lost hiker before dark. Infrastructure built to stand the test of time.
With more than 12,500 engineers in the making, we learn by building. We test it, break it and build it again, and we partner with the industries shaping what’s next.
Engineering the Future. It all starts at NC State.

entry.title: Radar Smaller Than a Thumbprint | NC State Research

media:group.media:title: Radar Smaller Than a Thumbprint | NC State Research
media:group.media:description:
Associate Professor Sevgi Zubeyde Gurbuz leads the Lab for Computational Intelligence for Radar (CI4R) at NC State. Her team develops physical AI algorithms that are effective, robust and low power on radar data.
The lab focuses on two problems. One is defending against drones by detecting their unique radar signatures. The other is radar-enabled cyber-physical human systems, which means putting radar on robots.
Today’s radars are smaller than a thumbprint. That opens the door to monitoring sleep and heart rate remotely, measuring gait and responding when someone falls.
Learn more about the lab: https://research.ece.ncsu.edu/ci4r/

entry.title: NAE President Tsu-Jae King Liu: Why Every Engineer Should Be an Optimist

media:group.media:title: NAE President Tsu-Jae King Liu: Why Every Engineer Should Be an Optimist
media:group.media:description:
NC State's College of Engineering welcomed National Academy of Engineering President Tsu-Jae King Liu for a talk on transforming engineering education. A fireside chat with Interim Dean Veena Misra followed, and it didn't hold back.
Liu, co-inventor of the FinFET transistor and Dean of UC Berkeley's College of Engineering, makes the case for why American engineering leadership matters now more than ever: the workforce shortage, the engineering completion-rate problem, the global race with China, and why she believes engineers should stay optimistic about the next 20 years.
Watch the full conversation, recorded June 30, 2026 at the James B. Hunt Jr. Library.
Speaker: Tsu-Jae King Liu, President, National Academy of Engineering Host: Veena Misra, Interim Dean, NC State College of Engineering

entry.title: 2026 O. Max Gardner Awardee: Dr. Richard Kim

media:group.media:title: 2026 O. Max Gardner Awardee: Dr. Richard Kim
media:group.media:description:
Youngsoo “Richard” Kim, Jimmy D. Clark Distinguished University Professor at North Carolina State University, is the 2026 recipient of the University of North Carolina System’s O. Max Gardner Award for his contributions to improving roadway infrastructure around the world.
The O. Max Gardner Award recognizes faculty who have “made the greatest contribution to the welfare of the human race.” It is the highest honor the UNC System’s Board of Governors confers on faculty and is the only award for which all faculty members across the 17 campuses are eligible. Kim, who is a professor in the Department of Civil, Construction and Environmental Engineering, is the 33rd faculty member from NC State to receive the award.

entry.title: Inside NC State’s NextG Wireless Lab: Building the Future of 6G

media:group.media:title: Inside NC State’s NextG Wireless Lab: Building the Future of 6G
media:group.media:description:
At NC State University, students are helping shape the future of wireless communication.
In this faculty spotlight, Vijay Shah, assistant professor of electrical and computer engineering, leads the NextG Wireless Lab on Centennial Campus. His team of students is advancing research in 5G, Open RAN and emerging 6G technologies, with a focus on RF systems, spectrum innovation and real-world applications.
Through hands-on experimentation and close collaboration with industry partners, students gain practical experience designing and testing next-generation wireless networks. From antennas and spectrum analyzers to prototype systems, the lab provides a foundation for solving complex challenges in connectivity.
This work prepares students to lead in both industry and academia, contributing to technologies that will connect billions of devices and transform how people communicate.

entry.title: Physical AI for Robotics | Edgar Lobaton | NC State Engineering Robotics Symposium

media:group.media:title: Physical AI for Robotics | Edgar Lobaton | NC State Engineering Robotics Symposium
media:group.media:description:
Edgar Lobaton, professor of electrical and computer engineering at NC State University, presents “What is Physical AI?” during the NC State Robotics Symposium at Hunt Library.
Lobaton’s research explores how artificial intelligence can interact with and operate within the physical world. His work focuses on robotics, computer vision and machine learning, developing systems that combine AI with physical and probabilistic modeling to improve how machines sense, interpret and respond to real-world environments. His research has applications ranging from wearable health monitoring and rehabilitation robotics to agricultural systems and autonomous sensing.
Lobaton leads the Active Robotic Sensing (ARoS) Laboratory at NC State and joined the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering in 2011. He received his Ph.D. in electrical engineering and computer sciences from the University of California, Berkeley. ￼
In this talk, Lobaton introduces the concept of physical AI and explains how physics-based simulations and robotics systems are shaping the next generation of intelligent machines that can operate safely and effectively in the real world.
This presentation was part of the NC State Robotics Symposium, which brings together researchers, students and industry partners to explore advances in robotics, artificial intelligence and autonomous systems.
